name: Interview behavioural questions, set 8
description: Spoken behavioural questions with model answers and rubrics: a corner nearly cut, a dull task, late help, a worry, a coin that is due, a wrong answer, no feedback and one number. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the corner you nearly cut.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a time you were tempted to cut a corner.
widget.model: As treasurer of my university chess society, I had to send our accounts to the students' union by a Friday. On the Wednesday I found my spreadsheet was £46 above the bank balance. The quick fix was to book the gap as sundry expenses and submit. Nobody would have checked. But next year's treasurer would inherit a number nobody could explain, and our grant depended on clean accounts. So I emailed the union for a three-day extension, which cost us our early-submission slot. Then I matched all 83 receipts against the bank statement, line by line. The gap was a refund I had entered twice. I corrected it, wrote a short note of what had happened, and submitted on the Monday. The cost was a weekend and a mildly annoyed union officer. Since then I reconcile the accounts every month rather than once a year, so any gap is small when I find it.

rubric.text: Names the shortcut and why it was tempting
Says who would have been affected had you taken it
What you did instead, with concrete steps
What doing it properly cost you, stated plainly
What you found, or the habit you keep now
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer is testing integrity under time pressure, so the temptation must be real. Name who would have paid for the shortcut, then say what the right choice cost you. A story with no cost reads as if there was no temptation.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the most boring task.

widget.prompt: Describe the most boring task you have had to do well.
widget.model: In my first summer I helped an ecology lab type up 1,400 handwritten field sheets from a ten-year bird survey. It was dull: the same eight columns, sheet after sheet, for three weeks. But the lab's trend analysis would use every row, and one wrong count for a rare species could fake a decline. So I set rules before I started. I typed in batches of fifty, then checked each batch against the paper by reading the numbers aloud backwards, which stopped me seeing what I expected. I added a column that flagged any count more than three times the site's average. Every Friday a postdoc re-entered twenty sheets at random and we compared. Over sixty sheets she found two errors, both in dates. I finished all 1,400 sheets, and the flags turned up eleven mistakes in the original paper records too. Dull work needs a checking system, not more willpower.

rubric.text: Says why the task mattered to someone else's work
The method you used to keep the error rate down
A count of what you got through, with the time it took
An error rate, measured by a check you set up
One lesson you would carry to similar work
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Careful work on dull tasks fills much of a junior quant's first year. Show why the task mattered, how you held the error rate down, and give counts. A checking system you designed is better evidence than a claim that you stayed focused.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: help you asked for late.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a time you asked for help later than you should have.
widget.model: In a second-year coursework group, my job was the code that stepped a heat equation forward in time. My results blew up after a few hundred steps. I was sure it was a typo, so I spent four evenings, about fourteen hours, rereading the code line by line. The sign I ignored was that no fix I tried changed anything, which meant I was looking in the wrong place. I did not ask because I felt the bug was my fault and my job to find. On the fifth day, with the deadline a week off, I took it to a teaching assistant. She asked what time step I used, and within ten minutes we saw it broke the stability limit for my grid. Halving the step fixed it. My group had lost four days of testing time. My rule now is two hours: if I am stuck that long with no new idea, I write the question down and ask someone.

rubric.text: States the problem and how long you worked alone, with the hours lost
Names the sign you ignored that you were stuck
Says honestly why you did not ask sooner
How the help solved it, and how quickly
A rule you use now, stated so someone could check it
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Firms want people who ask early, because a junior's lost day costs more than a senior's ten minutes. Count the hours, name the warning sign and give the cause honestly. End on a rule specific enough to follow, such as a time limit.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: what worries you about the job.

widget.prompt: What worries you about this job?
widget.model: What worries me is how slowly I will learn whether my work is any good. In my degree, feedback came within a week, on a marked problem sheet. The two researchers I spoke to at your open evening said a signal can take months to prove itself, and most ideas fail. I know this matters to me because of my dissertation. For six weeks I had no result, and I noticed my effort dropped when I could not see progress. I dealt with it then by setting weekly checks I could pass or fail, such as reproducing one table from a published paper. I would do the same here. In my first month I would ask my manager what a good first quarter looks like, and which small results the team uses to judge progress before anything trades. If there were none, I would want to know early, because that is the part of the job I would find hardest.

rubric.text: Names one real worry tied to the work itself, not to pay or hours
Gives evidence from your own past that the worry is real
What you did about it before, with a concrete step
How you would find out early whether it is a problem here
Shows you have learnt how the work runs, from a named source
Under 300 words

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: This tests self-knowledge and your grasp of the job. Pick a worry from the work, back it with your history and say how you would test it. A worry about hours or pay reads as a reason not to hire you.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: the coin that is due.

widget.prompt: I say: a fair coin has landed heads five times, so a tail is due. Put me right without being rude. You have two minutes.
widget.model: You are right that five heads in a row is unusual: with a fair coin it happens one time in 32. But that is the chance before any flips. The coin has no memory, so each flip is independent of the ones before. Given the five heads we have already seen, the next flip is heads with probability 1/2 and tails with probability 1/2. Here is another way to see it. Six flips can land 64 ways, all equally likely. Exactly two of those start with five heads, one ending in a head and one in a tail. So once we know the first five, a tail is exactly as likely as a head. If you would like to check it yourself, flip a coin a few hundred times, find every run of five heads, and count what comes next. You should see heads about half the time. The belief that a tail is due is common enough to have a name: the gambler's fallacy.

rubric.text: Agrees first with what is true: five heads is unlikely, with the number 1/32
States that the flips are independent, so a tail has chance 1/2
Gives a second way to see it, such as counting the 64 equally likely sequences
Offers a check the listener can run without trusting you
No word that blames or mocks the listener
Short enough for two minutes spoken: under 300 words

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The task is to correct a mistake while keeping the listener on side. Start with what they have right, give the independence point with the 1/2, then a check they can run. Naming the fallacy helps, provided it comes after the reasoning.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: an earlier answer was wrong.

widget.prompt: In your fourth interview of the day you realise an answer you gave in the second was wrong. What do you do?
widget.model: First I would finish the question in front of me properly. This interviewer deserves my full attention, and a rushed answer now would give them a second weak answer to mark. If the mistake kept nagging, I would jot one line on my notepad so I could let it go. I would wait for a natural point, usually when they ask if I have questions. Then I would say: in my second interview I said three heads in a row takes 6 flips on average, and I now think it is 14. Could you pass that on, or should I email the recruiter? That takes about twenty seconds. I would not apologise at length or rework the whole problem unless asked, because the point is to show I check my work, not to reopen the interview. Afterwards I would send the recruiter a short note with the corrected working, three or four lines. In a practice day last year I did exactly this, and the interviewer said it counted in my favour.

rubric.text: Finishes the current question before raising the old one
Corrects the earlier answer at a natural point, in a sentence or two
States the correction itself, not just that a mistake was made
No long apology and no reworking unless asked
A follow-up in writing to the recruiter or interviewer
Under 300 words

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Interviewers on a final day compare notes, so a corrected answer can count for you. Finish the current question, then correct the error briefly with the right figure. A long apology spends the time on your nerves rather than your work.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: rejected with no feedback.

widget.prompt: You are turned down after a final round and given no feedback. How do you work out what to change?
widget.model: On the evening of the final round I would write down every question from each of the four interviews, what I answered and how long I took, while it is fresh. Without feedback, that record is my evidence. Next I would mark each answer against what I know now: right or wrong, finished or not, and whether I needed hints. Last year, after a rejection, I did exactly this and found a pattern. I had solved every probability question but needed two hints in both coding rounds, so the weakest round was clear on the page, not just a feeling. I would also ask the recruiter once, politely, whether any feedback is possible, but I would not wait for it. Then I would choose one change, not five. That time it was timed coding practice: three problems a week at forty minutes each, with a date six weeks out to test myself again on problems from the same list.

rubric.text: A written record of each round, made the same day
Finds the weakest round by evidence such as hints or unfinished answers
Asks once for feedback without depending on it
Chooses one change, stated concretely
A date or deadline to check whether the change worked
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: This tests whether you learn from failure without a teacher. A same-day written record turns a vague feeling into evidence, and the weakest round should be found from it. One concrete change with a date beats a promise to work harder on everything.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: one number for your project.

widget.prompt: Give me the one number that sums up your project, and tell me how it could mislead.
widget.model: My dissertation forecast a regional grid's electricity demand one day ahead. The number is 3.1 per cent: the mean absolute error on the final year, which the model never saw, against 4.6 per cent for the baseline of using the same day last week. That is about a third less error. It could mislead in two ways. First, the test year was mild, with no long cold spell, so the model never faced the days that matter most to a grid operator. Second, an average hides the worst days: on the 20 days of highest demand my error was 7.8 per cent, not much better than the baseline's 8.5. So beside the 3.1 I would show the error on those peak days and a chart of error by month, and say plainly that I have not tested the model in a hard winter. With another month, I would hold out the cold winter three years earlier and test on that instead.

rubric.text: States the number with its unit, its test set and its baseline
A first way the number flatters the work, specific to the project
A second, different way it flatters, with a figure
What you would show beside the number to correct the picture
Says plainly what has not been tested
Under 300 words

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer wants to see you distrust your own headline. Give the number with its unit, test set and baseline, then two separate ways it overstates the work. Ending on what you would show beside it proves you would report it honestly.
